title: Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge for Lawn and turf care
audience: Owners of small Australian lawn and turf businesses who need a base rate and a minimum charge before quoting
learningOutcomes: Separate billable hours from non-billable hours, and calculate the time available to bill.
Calculate a base hourly rate from the owner's own costs and income target, then compare it with local evidence.
Set a minimum charge for short visits, and explain it to a client before the visit.

instruction.heading: Factors that move the rate
instruction.body: A rate depends on skill, experience, how scarce the skill is locally, the range of services offered and the cost of running the round. A lawn owner who can mow, edge, blow and check a sprinkler in one visit can justify a higher rate than one who only mows, because the client saves a second visit. Use local evidence rather than a national average. In Melbourne, the cost guide lists a gardener at $47, $68 and $105 per hour, GST included (What's the Damage, updated November 2026). Treat that as a reference point, not as your rate. Council work is often priced on a schedule of rates rather than one hourly figure. The Central Coast Council (Tasmania) tender is priced that way and lists mowing, weeding, fertilising, turf care and irrigation maintenance.

instruction.heading: Counting the hours that can be billed
instruction.body: Few paid hours are billable. Travel between lawns, quoting, admin, marketing, equipment upkeep, sick days and leave are not billable. Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract the non-billable time. A Jobber guide puts billable time at about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, which is a general range rather than an Australian figure (Jobber, 5 November 2024, modified 20 July 2026). If only 60 of every 100 paid hours are billable, the costs of all 100 hours must be recovered from 60, so the rate is about 1.67 times the rate for a fully billable week (100 divided by 60).

instruction.heading: Building the rate from costs and income
instruction.body: Add the annual costs of running the round, including insurance, registration, mower and trimmer upkeep, the vehicle, phone, software, marketing and accounting, to the income you need. business.gov.au says on-costs such as superannuation, leave and tax belong in the hourly figure (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026). Have a registered tax agent confirm how leave and superannuation apply to your situation before the rate is published. Divide the total by billable hours to reach the base rate, then review it about every three months and compare it with what clients accept (Business Victoria, undated).

instruction.heading: Setting a minimum charge for short visits
instruction.body: Short visits can cost more in time than they earn, because travel and set-up do not shrink with the size of the lawn. A minimum charge covers the visit and must be stated before the visit. One method takes the full cost of the visit, divides it by one minus the target margin, and makes the minimum cover travel, set-up and admin (Contractor+, 23 September 2026; the figures on that page are illustrative and only the method is used here). For example, if the full visit cost is $40 (illustrative) and the target margin is 30 per cent, the minimum is $57.14. The cost guide's small-lawn visit starts at $47 (GST included); that is a market point, not a rule for your minimum. No sourced Australian Consumer Law or Victorian rule on minimum or call-out charges was found, so check before publishing a price sheet.

procedure: Estimate the paid working hours in a year, then subtract travel, admin, marketing, training and leave to find the billable hours.
List the annual running costs, including insurance, registration, equipment, vehicle, phone, software and marketing.
Add the income needed, including allowances for leave and tax confirmed by a registered tax agent.
Divide the total by the billable hours to find the base rate.
Set a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin for a short visit, and state it in writing.
Review the rate each quarter, and record any change and the reason for it.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative: an owner's log shows that only 60 of every 100 paid hours can be billed, but the owner plans to set the rate as if every paid hour could be billed.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the effect on the rate if the wrong assumption is kept?
workedExamples.reasoning: Pricing as if every paid hour were billable understates the rate, because the costs and the income still have to come out of the hours that can be billed. With 60 billable hours in every 100, the rate would be about 40 per cent below the level the costs require (60 divided by 100 is 0.6). The rate must be built from billable hours, then checked against the local evidence and the minimum charge before it is published.

commonErrors.error: Setting a rate from a published average or a competitor's figure without checking the costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Build the base rate from the owner's own costs and billable hours, then compare it with local evidence.

commonErrors.error: Pricing as though every paid hour could be billed.
commonErrors.prevention: Subtract the non-billable time before dividing.

commonErrors.error: Taking short visits at the same rate, without covering travel and set-up.
commonErrors.prevention: Set and state a minimum charge that covers travel, set-up and admin.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Price display rules come from the Australian Consumer Law. Misleading price statements are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). The sources read for this variant do not cover minimum or call-out charges, or what counts as a fair term. Check those points against current ACCC guidance or a legal adviser before publishing a price sheet.
Confirm how leave and superannuation apply to the owner's own pay with a registered tax agent before the rate is published.

qualityStandard: Billable hours are calculated from a logged or estimated month, not assumed.
The base rate is built from the owner's costs and income target, and is compared with local evidence.
A minimum charge is set and stated before any short visit.
documentationEvidence: Annual costs and income worksheet, with the source and date of each cost
Billable hours calculation showing the non-billable deductions
Price sheet showing the base rate, the minimum charge and the review date
summary: Price from billable hours, not from paid hours.
Build the rate from costs and a stated income target, then check it against local evidence.
Set and state a minimum charge for short visits.

knowledgeChecks.question: An owner can bill only some of the paid hours. How should the rate be built?
options: From all paid hours, so the rate looks lower and so the client pays less per job
From billable hours, so the costs and income are covered by the work that can be billed
From the average published on a website and from the rate listed by the nearest competitor
From the rate the owner wishes the market would pay and the owner's own mood on the day

knowledgeChecks.question: Why set a minimum charge for short lawn visits?
options: Because short visits need travel but no set-up time at all and the admin takes no time
Because travel, set-up and admin time does not shrink with the size of the job
Because clients expect every job to cost the same amount, whatever its size
Because a minimum charge replaces a written quote for every job the owner takes

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the best source for checking a base hourly rate?
options: A single published national average from the largest trade body
The owner's own costs and billable hours, compared with local evidence
A friend's rate, without checking the costs or the local market
The rate shown on the first page of a bidding site this week

sourceReferences: business.gov.au, 'Choose a pricing strategy', https://business.gov.au/products-and-services/choose-a-pricing-strategy, page metadata dated 1 October 2026. Supports: on-costs such as super, leave and tax belong in the hourly cost; going-rate pricing as one check.

Jobber, 'What are billable hours', https://getjobber.com/academy/what-are-billable-hours/, published 5 November 2024, last modified 20 July 2026. General range, not an Australian figure. Supports: billable time typically 60 to 80 per cent of working hours.

Contractor+, 'Minimum Service Call Charge: A Contractor's Pricing Guide', https://contractorplus.app/blog/minimum-service-call-charge, 23 September 2026. Figures labelled illustrative and not market rates; no country stated. Only the method is used: minimum from full visit cost divided by one minus target margin.

Business Victoria, 'Develop a pricing strategy', https://business.vic.gov.au/business-information/finance/pricing-for-profit/develop-a-pricing-strategy, no date shown. Supports: review prices about every three months.

What's the Damage, 'Lawn mowing cost Melbourne', https://whatsthedamage.com.au/lawn-mowing-cost-melbourne/, verified 1 November 2026, updated November 2026. Cost guide, not a regulator; GST included. Supports: gardener hourly $47 / $68 / $105; small-lawn visit from $47.

Central Coast Council (Tasmania) gardening services tender, https://www.australiantenders.com.au/tenders/597825/triennial-tenders-2026-2028-gardening-services, closing 10 November 2025. Supports: priced on a schedule of rates; scope includes mowing, weeding, fertilising, turf care and irrigation maintenance.
